subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 5 periods = 200 minutes
Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

periods.activity_title: Cracking the Mystery Box — Arrays Reveal Factors

tasks_in_class.description: Guess the multiplier from four numbers coming out of the box; determine if more than one multiplier is possible; identify what numbers were put inside.
Make different arrays for 10, 14, 13, 20, 25, 32, 37, 46, 54 and identify the factors in each case.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the mystery-box idea: a number goes in, a larger number comes out — what is the hidden multiplier? Pose Find the hidden numbers. (a)(b)(c), p.164 ("Guess the multiplier from four numbers coming out....") orally. Children share guesses and debate whether one multiplier or many could work, surfacing the idea that factors are multipliers.

Children use square tiles or grid paper to build every possible rectangle for each number in Let Us Do (a)–(i), p.165 ("Make different arrays for 10, 14, 13, 20, 25...."). Each rectangle's side lengths are listed as a factor pair. Pairs share their arrays; the class notices that 13 and 37 yield only one non-trivial arrangement — an unhurried class discussion names these as numbers with exactly two factors.

Groups continue Let Us Do (a)–(i), p.165 for the remaining numbers (32, 46, 54), recording all factor pairs in a table. A quick count round the class compiles the list of factors for each number on the board, letting children see how array count signals the number of factor pairs.

Whole-class consolidation: children describe in their own words what a factor is, using one of their arrays as evidence. Teacher poses: 'Can 1 always be a factor?' — children verify by drawing a 1 × n array, closing the unit on firm conceptual ground.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes conflate the array's total squares with the factor — prompt them to name the two side lengths, not the area. When 13 and 37 yield only a 1 × n array, resist naming 'prime' immediately; let the observation emerge from the array evidence. Square tiles or centimetre grid paper make the concrete link strongest.
materials: Square tiles or centimetre grid paper

section_titles: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
periods.activity_title: Rabbit and Frog Race — Landing on Common Ground

tasks_in_class.description: Rabbit jumps 4 each time, frog jumps 3; use the number line to find numbers both animals will touch — common multiples of 3 and 4.
Spider jumps 3 every time, grasshopper jumps 6; use the number line to find the common multiples of 3 and 6.
Robby rabbit jumps 4, Deeku deer jumps 6, both start at 0; will both reach the food at the end of the road? Who reaches first? Explain.
Mowgli jumps by 2 steps from 0 along a winding trail; identify which of his friends (at marked positions) he will be able to visit.

homework.description: Find 5 common multiples for each of the following pairs: 2&3, 5&8, 2&4, 3&9, 5&10, 9&12, 8&12, 6&8, 6&9.

time_bands.activity: Set up a number line on the floor (0–24) using tape or drawn on the board. Two children act as rabbit (jumps of 4) and frog (jumps of 3) for Animal Jumps, p.165 ("Rabbit jumps 4 each time, frog jumps 3; find numbers both touch...."). The class marks shared landing squares in a different colour, naming them common multiples of 3 and 4.

Repeat with Animal Jumps (spider/grasshopper), p.166 ("Spider jumps 3 every time, grasshopper jumps 6...."). Children predict before jumping: will spider land wherever grasshopper does? After acting it out they list common multiples of 3 and 6, noticing every multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 3 — an unhurried pair discussion surfaces this pattern.

Groups work on Let Us Do Q2, p.167 ("Robby rabbit jumps 4, Deeku deer jumps 6; will both reach the food? Who reaches first?..."). Children list multiples of 4 and 6 side by side to find common landing points and argue their reasoning in writing or speech.

Children tackle Let Us Do Q3, p.167 ("Mowgli jumps by 2 steps; identify which friends he visits....") individually, applying their understanding that Mowgli can only reach even-numbered positions. Close by assigning Let Us Do Q1 (a)–(h), p.166 ("Find 5 common multiples for each pair....") as take-home practice.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes list any multiple of either number rather than multiples shared by both — the physical jump activity, with two colours, corrects this concretely before moving to symbolic listing. The spider-grasshopper pair is intentionally easier, building confidence before Q2's reasoning demand. Additional practice from the pairs exercise is assigned as homework so in-class time focuses on the conceptual jump tasks.
materials: Floor number line (tape, 0–24) or large drawn number line
Two coloured chalk or sticky dots to mark jump landings

section_titles: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
periods.activity_title: Mowgli's Trail — Which Jump Reaches Every Friend?

tasks_in_class.description: On Mowgli's trail, identify which friends he meets jumping by 3 steps; confirm 3 is a common factor of the positions landed on.
Find common factors of 24 and 36 by testing jump sizes 2, 3, 4; find other jumps that reach both; list all common factors; check jump of 1.
What are the common factors of 12 and 13?
From the numbers 0, 10, 16, 27, 36, 48 on a number line, find which can be reached by jumps of 4; complete '4 is the common factor of ___'.

time_bands.activity: Draw Mowgli's trail on the board with friends at various positions. Children work on Mowgli trail — jump by 3, p.168 ("Identify which friends Mowgli meets jumping by 3...."). They list the positions reached and complete the statement '3 is a common factor of ___', making the reversal from multiple-finding to factor-finding explicit.

Groups work through Let Us Do Q4 (a)–(f), p.168 ("Find common factors of 24 and 36 by testing jump sizes 2, 3, 4...."). Each group tests one jump size and reports; the class builds a complete list of common factors together, then verifies that jump of 1 always works, discussing why.

Children attempt Let Us Do Q5, p.168 ("What are the common factors of 12 and 13?") individually, then share findings. The result — only 1 — connects directly to the array work built on in the first unit, where 13 had only a 1 × n array.

Whole class works Let Us Do Q6, p.169 ("From numbers 0, 10, 16, 27, 36, 48; find which are reached by jumps of 4...."). Children mark the number line, test each number, and complete the sentence. Teacher asks: 'Why is 27 not reached?' — probing the link between divisibility and factor membership.

periods.teacher_notes: The conceptual shift here is from 'what do I land on?' to 'what jump size reaches a given set of positions?' — this reversal often needs the trail drawn visibly so children can test each jump size concretely. Q5 is purposefully brief; use it to link back to the arrays for 12 and 13 built earlier, where the difference in factor count was already visible. Additional practice tasks T-9 and T-10 (Mowgli trail jumps by 5 and by 10) can be used as quick individual practice if time allows; they are noted as such in the teacher guide.
materials: Board with Mowgli's trail drawn (positions 0–60 with friends labelled)

section_titles: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
periods.activity_title: True or False, Then Solve — Testing Factor Reasoning

tasks_in_class.description: Find the common factors of eight pairs: 12&16, 8&12, 4&16, 2&9, 3&5, 12&15, 20&5, 9&21, 6&27.

State True or False: factors of even numbers must be even; multiples of odd numbers cannot be even; factors of odd numbers cannot be even; one common multiple of two consecutive numbers is their product; the only common factor of consecutive numbers is 1; 0 cannot be a factor.
Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day, Bagheera every 5th day; if both start on the same day, on which days will they hunt together?
Mowgli wants to visit Baloo at position 30 but avoid Sher Khan at 25; how long (in steps) could each jump be?
What jump size lets Mowgli meet both Kaa at position 21 and Akela at position 35?

time_bands.activity: Children work in pairs on Let Us Do Q7 (a)–(h), p.169 ("Find the common factors of eight pairs: 12&16, 8&12...."). Each pair handles two or three pairs, then shares results; the class checks by asking 'does this number divide both without remainder?' — reinforcing the jump-size meaning of a factor.

Whole class works through Let Us Do Q8 (a)–(f), p.169 ("State True or False: factors of even numbers must be even;....") as a discussion activity. For each statement, one child defends True and another defends False before the class decides, using counter-examples drawn from the factor lists they have been building.

Children individually solve Let Us Do Q9, p.169 ("Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day, Bagheera every 5th day; on which days together?..."). They list multiples of 3 and 5 to find common hunting days, writing their answer as a list.

Groups work on Let Us Do Q10(a) and Q10(b), p.169 ("Mowgli visits Baloo at 30, avoids Sher Khan at 25..."; "what jump size reaches Kaa at 21 and Akela at 35?..."). Children identify factors of each target number and apply the common-factor idea to find valid jump sizes, sharing reasoning aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: The True/False task in Q8 is a rich reasoning exercise; children frequently assert that factors of odd numbers cannot be even without testing — directing them to find all factors of 9 or 15 concretely resolves the confusion. For Q10(b), students need to find a common factor of 21 and 35; the factor-listing method built through this section gives them the tool, and 7 should emerge naturally from their lists.
materials: Number lines (0–50) for the word problems

periods.activity_title: Sort the Numbers — Venn Diagram Divisibility

tasks_in_class.description: Sort 90, 45, 84, 22, 66, 56, 38, 78, 25, 30, 62, 95, 75, 40, 55 into a Venn diagram: divisible by 2 only, 5 only, 10 only, or 2 & 5 & 10.

time_bands.activity: Draw a large three-circle Venn diagram on the board (circles labelled: divisible by 2, divisible by 5, divisible by 10). Introduce the divisibility rules: last digit even → divisible by 2; last digit 0 or 5 → divisible by 5; last digit 0 → divisible by 10. Test two or three numbers together (e.g. 30, 22, 45) as a class, placing each in the diagram and noting that 30 belongs where all three circles overlap.

Groups each receive a set of number cards from the fifteen numbers in Let Us Do Q11 (a)–(d), p.170 ("Sort 90, 45, 84, 22, 66, 56, 38, 78, 25, 30, 62, 95, 75, 40, 55 into a Venn diagram...."). Each group places their cards in the diagram drawn on their paper, justifying each placement by naming the last digit and the rule it triggers. Groups compare placements and resolve disagreements.

Whole-class consolidation of Let Us Do Q11, p.170. The class builds one agreed Venn diagram on the board. Children explain: which region is always empty (divisible by 10 but not by 2 or 5 — impossible), and why any number divisible by 10 must also appear in both the 2 and 5 circles. This surfaces the relationship between the three rules as a generalisation.

Children individually write two numbers of their own choice — one that belongs in the overlapping region of all three circles and one that belongs in divisible-by-5-only — and verify each using the rules. A quick count round the class checks their choices, closing the unit on student-generated examples.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often place numbers divisible by 10 in the 10-only region, missing that 10 is always a multiple of both 2 and 5; the Venn diagram makes this overlap unavoidable once they check both rules for the same number. The factor-and-multiple work built through the chapter gives children a strong grounding for understanding why these divisibility rules work — a jump of 2 reaches every even number, a jump of 5 reaches every number ending in 0 or 5, so divisibility by 10 demands both. Prompt children to connect last-digit checking to the factor idea they already know.
materials: Large Venn diagram drawn on board (three overlapping circles)
Number cards (15 numbers from Q11) — one set per group

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: A cat jumps 4 steps at a time and a dog jumps 5 steps at a time. Both start at 0 on a number line. Mark the first three numbers where both animals land. What do we call these numbers?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Both land on 20 and 40 (and 60). The first three common landing numbers are 20, 40, and 60. These are called common multiples of 4 and 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 4 (4, 8, 12, 16, 20 …) and multiples of 5 (5, 10, 15, 20 …) and find numbers that appear in both lists.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child physically hop two fingers along the number line, one for each animal; stretch: find the next two common multiples beyond 60.

exercise.description: Rabbit jumps 4 each time, frog jumps 3; use the number line to find numbers both animals will touch — common multiples of 3 and 4.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: A spider jumps 4 steps every time and a beetle jumps 8 steps every time. Which of the following is a number where both insects always land?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 16. Both 4 and 8 divide 16 exactly (4 × 4 = 16; 8 × 2 = 16), so both insects land on 16.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the number is a multiple of both 4 and 8 by dividing each and confirming no remainder.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 12 shows the child checked only multiples of 4 (4 × 3 = 12) without verifying 8 also lands there (12 ÷ 8 = 1 remainder 4).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 20 shows the child checked only multiples of 4 (4 × 5 = 20) without verifying 8 also lands there (20 ÷ 8 = 2 remainder 4).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 28 shows the child checked only multiples of 4 (4 × 7 = 28) without verifying 8 also lands there (28 ÷ 8 = 3 remainder 4).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child draw both jump sequences on a number line and circle shared landings; stretch: list the next two common multiples of 4 and 8 beyond 16.

exercise.description: Spider jumps 3 every time, grasshopper jumps 6; use the number line to find the common multiples of 3 and 6.

items.prompt: Sana puts a number into a mystery box. Four numbers come out: 6, 9, 15, 21. What is the hidden multiplier? Is there more than one possible multiplier? Explain how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The hidden multiplier is 3, because 6 = 3 × 2, 9 = 3 × 3, 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7. There is exactly one multiplier (3) since 3 is the only number that divides all four outputs exactly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the number that divides all four outputs without remainder — that is the common factor, which is the hidden multiplier.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write each output as a multiplication sentence (__ × __ = 6) and look for the factor that appears in all; stretch: ask the child to create their own mystery-box output set with a hidden multiplier of 4.

exercise.description: Guess the multiplier from four numbers coming out of the box; determine if more than one multiplier is possible; identify what numbers were put inside.

items.prompt: Ritu tries to make rectangular arrays for the number 17. How many different arrays can she make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Only one array (1 × 17). Because 17 has exactly two factors (1 and 17), only a single rectangle with those side lengths is possible.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test each number from 1 to 17 as a possible side length; only 1 divides 17 without remainder (other than 17 itself), giving one unique rectangle shape.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Counting 1 × 17 and 17 × 1 as different shows the child has not recognised that rotating a rectangle gives the same factor pair.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing three arrays shows the child may be guessing based on the number of digits rather than testing divisibility.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing four arrays suggests the child may be confusing 17 with a composite number such as 16 or 18 that has more factor pairs.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the child use square tiles and physically attempt to arrange 17 tiles into rows and columns, discovering that only a 1-row arrangement works; stretch: ask which other numbers up to 20 give only one array.

exercise.description: Make different arrays for 10, 14, 13, 20, 25, 32, 37, 46, 54 and identify the factors in each case.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: A deer jumps 6 steps and a rabbit jumps 4 steps, both starting at 0. The food is at position 24. Will both animals reach the food? Which animal reaches position 24 first? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, both reach 24. Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24 — deer reaches 24 in 4 jumps. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 — rabbit reaches 24 in 6 jumps. 24 is a common multiple of both 4 and 6. The deer reaches 24 first (in fewer jumps).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of each jump size and check whether 24 appears in both lists; count how many jumps each animal needs.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a number line to 30 and ask them to mark each animal's jumps in a different colour; stretch: ask the child to find the next position beyond 24 where both animals land together.

exercise.description: Robby rabbit jumps 4, Deeku deer jumps 6, both start at 0; will both reach the food at the end of the road? Who reaches first? Explain.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: Mowgli's friends are at positions 18 and 30 on a trail. List all the jump sizes that let Mowgli land exactly on both positions. What do we call these jump sizes?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. Factors of 30: 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30. Jump sizes that reach both: 1, 2, 3, 6. These are the common factors of 18 and 30.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factors of each number separately, then identify the numbers that appear in both lists — these are the common factors.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to divide 18 and 30 by 1, 2, 3 in turn and check each; stretch: ask which of the common factors is the greatest, and why that jump size is useful.

exercise.description: Find common factors of 24 and 36 by testing jump sizes 2, 3, 4; find other jumps that reach both; list all common factors; check jump of 1.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: Which statement about factors and multiples is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Factors of every even number must themselves be even.

options.label: B
options.text: The only common factor of two consecutive numbers is 1.

options.label: C
options.text: Multiples of odd numbers can never be even.

options.label: D
options.text: 0 is a factor of every number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The only common factor of two consecutive numbers is 1. Any two consecutive numbers share no common divisor greater than 1 because consecutive numbers differ by 1, and a number greater than 1 cannot divide two numbers that differ by 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Test a pair of consecutive numbers (e.g. 8 and 9): factors of 8 are 1, 2, 4, 8; factors of 9 are 1, 3, 9; only 1 is shared — confirm this holds generally.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this shows the child has overgeneralised; counter-example: 3 is a factor of 6, but 3 is odd.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this shows the child has confused 'odd number' with 'odd multiple'; 3 × 2 = 6, which is even.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this shows a misconception about 0; division by 0 is undefined, so 0 cannot be a factor.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to list all factors of two small consecutive numbers (e.g. 4 and 5) and circle what is shared; stretch: ask them to write their own True/False statement about factors and give a counter-example for the false one.

exercise.description: State True or False: factors of even numbers must be even; multiples of odd numbers cannot be even; factors of odd numbers cannot be even; one common multiple of two consecutive numbers is their product; the only common factor of consecutive numbers is 1; 0 cannot be a factor.

items.prompt: Priya says: 'Any number divisible by 10 is also divisible by 2 and by 5.' Is Priya correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because a number divisible by 10 ends in 0, so it is even (divisible by 2) and ends in 0 or 5 (divisible by 5).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because divisibility by 10 is a separate rule that does not depend on 2 or 5.

options.label: C
options.text: Only sometimes — it depends on whether the number is large or small.

options.label: D
options.text: No, because some numbers divisible by 10 are odd.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. Any number divisible by 10 ends in 0. Ending in 0 satisfies the divisibility rule for 2 (last digit even) and the rule for 5 (last digit 0 or 5). So divisibility by 10 always implies divisibility by both 2 and 5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the last-digit rules for 2 and 5 to a number ending in 0, and verify both conditions are met simultaneously.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this shows the child has memorised the three rules as separate facts without connecting them through the last-digit pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this shows the child believes divisibility depends on the size of the number rather than on a fixed last-digit rule.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this shows a fundamental misconception — the child may believe multiples of 10 can be odd, not recognising that all multiples of 10 end in 0 and are therefore even.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write three multiples of 10 and check the last digit for each; stretch: ask whether a number can be divisible by 2 and by 5 without being divisible by 10, and give an example or counter-example.

exercise.description: Sort 90, 45, 84, 22, 66, 56, 38, 78, 25, 30, 62, 95, 75, 40, 55 into a Venn diagram: divisible by 2 only, 5 only, 10 only, or 2 & 5 & 10.

items.section_title: Common multiples via animal number-line jumps
items.prompt: Which of the following is a common multiple of 3 and 7?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 21. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 … Multiples of 7: 7, 14, 21 … Both lists include 21.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 3 and multiples of 7 until a number appears in both lists.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 14 shows the child recognised a multiple of 7 but did not check whether 14 is also a multiple of 3 (14 ÷ 3 = 4 remainder 2).
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 27 shows the child recognised a multiple of 3 but did not check whether 27 is also a multiple of 7 (27 ÷ 7 = 3 remainder 6).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 35 shows the child recognised a multiple of 7 (and of 5) but did not check whether 35 is a multiple of 3 (35 ÷ 3 = 11 remainder 2).

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a partially completed table of multiples of 3 and 7 and ask them to circle shared entries; stretch: find the next two common multiples of 3 and 7 after 21.

exercise.description: Find 5 common multiples for each of the following pairs: 2&3, 5&8, 2&4, 3&9, 5&10, 9&12, 8&12, 6&8, 6&9.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: What are the common factors of 20 and 30?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factors of each number and identify those that appear in both lists.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this shows the child included 4 (a factor of 20 only) and missed that 4 does not divide 30 exactly.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this shows the child included 3 (a factor of 30 only) and missed that 3 does not divide 20 exactly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this shows the child omitted 1 (every pair of numbers shares 1 as a common factor) and included 20, which does not divide 30 exactly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to write out all factors of 20 and 30 using the jump model — which jump sizes reach 20? Which reach 30? Circle those that reach both; stretch: ask which common factor is the greatest and explain what that tells you about dividing both numbers equally.

exercise.description: Find the common factors of eight pairs: 12&16, 8&12, 4&16, 2&9, 3&5, 12&15, 20&5, 9&21, 6&27.

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: Rani waters her plants every 4 days and feeds them every 6 days. She does both on Day 1. On which day will she first water and feed the plants on the same day again?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Day 13. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12 … Multiples of 6: 6, 12 … The first common multiple is 12, so she does both again on Day 1 + 12 = Day 13.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List multiples of 4 and multiples of 6 to find their smallest common multiple, then add 1 (the starting day) to get the answer.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the child a number line and ask them to mark multiples of 4 with one colour and multiples of 6 with another, then find the first shared mark; stretch: ask on which day she will do both for the second time.

exercise.description: Sher Khan hunts every 3rd day, Bagheera every 5th day; if both start on the same day, on which days will they hunt together?

items.section_title: Common factors via jump model and divisibility
items.prompt: Mowgli wants to visit Raju at position 28 and Meena at position 42 on a trail. What is the largest jump size that lands exactly on both positions?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 7. Factors of 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28. Factors of 42: 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 14, 21, 42. Common factors: 1, 2, 7, 14. The largest is 14. Wait — recheck: 14 divides 28 exactly (28 ÷ 14 = 2) and 14 divides 42 exactly (42 ÷ 14 = 3). The largest common factor is 14.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all factors of 28 and 42, identify those in both lists, and select the largest.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the child to test jump sizes 1, 2, 7, 14 one at a time by dividing both 28 and 42; stretch: ask what the largest jump size would be if the two positions were 36 and 48.

exercise.description: What jump size lets Mowgli meet both Kaa at position 21 and Akela at position 35?
